Consider adding an explicit USE THIS TOOL FOR / DO NOT USE FOR block to the tool description, mirroring the pattern in [cost_optimization_hub_tools](https://github.com/awslabs/mcp/blob/main/src/billing-cost-management-mcp-server/awslabs/billing_cost_management_mcp_server/tools/cost_optimization_hub_tools.py#L55-L62) and [compute_optimizer_tools](https://github.com/awslabs/mcp/blob/main/src/billing-cost-management-mcp-server/awslabs/billing_cost_management_mcp_server/tools/compute_optimizer_tools.py#L42-L50)

The names are extremely close (`compute-optimizer` vs `compute-optimizer-automation` vs `cost-optimization-hub`) and the "recommended_action" concept overlaps with compute-optimizer's per-resource recommendations — without a disambiguation block, agents may pick the wrong tool for questions like "what EBS changes are recommended?"

Could you also test will agent get confused about the 3 tools?

**Bug (medium): `describe_canaries()` is not paginated**

`synthetics.describe_canaries` returns a `NextToken` and is paged. Default page size is 20; max is 100. For any account with more canaries than the default page, this silently misses the rest — the tool will confidently claim "All N canaries are healthy" while ignoring the ones on page 2.

Suggested:

```python
all_canaries = []
next_token = None
while True:
    kwargs = {'MaxResults': 100}
    if next_token:

    describe_resp = synthetics_client.describe_canaries(**kwargs)
    all_canaries.extend(describe_resp.get('Canaries', []))
    next_token = describe_resp.get('NextToken')
    if not next_token:
        break
```

You probably also want an upper cap (e.g. stop at ~200 canaries and tell the user to narrow the scope) so auto-discovery cannot accidentally fan out over a huge inventory.

**Bug (medium): `MaxResults=100` with no `NextToken` loop → false negatives**

`list_services` returns a `NextToken`; this single call caps at 100 results. If the account has more than 100 services during the window, any named target that happens to live beyond the first page silently falls through — `by_name.get(name)` returns `None`, nothing gets flagged, and the user sees no warning for a target that is actually uninstrumented.

Every other error response added in this review wave adopts `{'error': ..., 'error_type': 'bad_request' | 'service_error' | 'internal_error'}` (rum_tools.py:438, 440, 600, 645, 706, 730, 784, ...). This helper emits `'error'` but no `error_type`.

return json.dumps({
